question: A programme sponsor asks who is accountable for the requirements catalogue now that most of it is drafted with Claude. Which answer best reflects sound practice?
options: A) The named business owner still signs it off; Claude speeds the drafting but cannot carry accountability.
B) The analyst who wrote the prompts signs it off, since they know best how the catalogue was put together.
C) Claude signs the catalogue off, and the business owner reviews only the items Claude marks as uncertain.
D) Sign-off can wait while the catalogue is a draft, because every item will be reviewed again in delivery.
correct_answers: A) The named business owner still signs it off; Claude speeds the drafting but cannot carry accountability.
explanations: Correct. Delegating the drafting does not move the accountability. The business owner remains the person who can commit to the requirements being right, and keeping sign-off there is what makes the faster drafting safe to rely on.

Knowing how the catalogue was produced is not the same as being able to commit the business to it. Prompt authorship is a process detail; sign-off is a statement that these are the needs the organisation will fund.
A tool cannot be accountable for a commitment the organisation makes, and reviewing only self-flagged items means the errors Claude is confident about, which are the dangerous ones, go unexamined.

Deferring sign-off pushes accountability into a phase where changing a requirement is far more expensive. Delivery review checks whether the build matches the catalogue, not whether the catalogue was ever right.
